title: Hooks: controlling execution before and after actions

opening.headline: If you want to block it definitively with code just before calling the tool, find out where to hang the hook and how to return the result.
body: Let's say the agent wants to run a destructive shell command like rm -rf. Even if the prompt says "don't use dangerous commands" there's no guarantee that the model will always follow. Regardless of the model's judgment, a device is needed where the code intervenes just before the tool is executed to definitively block it.

In this class, we will look at when Claude Code's hooks are executed, how the settings are structured, and how the results are returned as an exit code and JSON. Then, we set a standard to distinguish between what to block with hooks and what to block with permission rules, and compare where ADK's callbacks and inference hooks are located.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the type of hook and when it is executed
You can distinguish between blocking with hooks and blocking with permission rules.

screens.title: I want to block it with a rule right before calling the tool.
screens.lead: By alternating between the two states, compare asking with a prompt and intervening with code.

visual.alt: A flow in which a hook is inserted after the model decides to call a tool but before execution.

states.label: Ask with prompt
states.body: The method is to write “Do not use dangerous commands such as rm -rf” at the system prompt. In most cases the model is followed, but there is no guarantee that it will always be followed. Instructions can get lost in long conversations, ambiguous requests, or instructions in external content can cause the model to change its judgment. If you violate it even once, the file will be deleted, and the only way to check if you violated it is to read the model's response.

states.label: Intervene with code
states.body: Just before the tool is executed, the code I created reads the call and definitively blocks it. Whatever the model decides, the code's decision takes precedence, so calls that break the rules are not executed. What you want is this deterministic device that operates independently of the model's judgment, and in Claude Code we call this a hook.

screens.outro: The core question of this lesson is this. At what point, what information do you receive, and how can you prevent it?

screens.title: Think about it: Moments you want to intervene before and after execution
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever wanted to automatically run a formatter on an agent-edited file?
items.answer: These requests are post-processing that occurs after the tool has run. Instead of asking your model to run the formatter every time, you can have it run automatically immediately after a successful file edit so you don't miss anything.

items.prompt: Have you ever wanted to block a specific folder or command under any circumstances?
items.answer: In any situation, what needs to be prevented should be enforced through code rather than left to the judgment of the model. By intervening just before the tool runs, you can prevent whatever reason the model decided to make that call.

items.prompt: Have you ever wished that your environment information was automatically populated when a session starts?
items.answer: The hook is also executed when the session starts. The breadth of the hook extends to not only invoking tools but also being able to intervene at multiple points in the session and turn. In this lesson, we will focus on the front and back of tool calls.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's start by defining what a hook is.

screens.title: What is a Hook
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: A hook is a user-defined action that runs automatically at a predefined point in the Claude Code lifecycle. handler comes in five types: command executes shell commands, http sends a POST request, mcp_tool invokes tools from the MCP (external tool integration specification) server, prompt allows the model to evaluate once, and agent executes subordinate agents. When an event occurs and matcher matches, the event's JSON context is passed to handler. A command hook accepts input via stdin and returns results to exit code and stdout. Since the same hook event can occur in a terminal, IDE, desktop app, or cloud session, a single hook can be reused across multiple environments.

terms.tip: This is the action that is actually executed when an event occurs. There are five types: command, http, mcp_tool, prompt, and agent.
This is a condition that filters out what the hook will respond to. Tool events are based on the tool name; if they don't match, the hook won't run.
This is JSON containing event information. If it is a tool event, it contains the tool name and input arguments so the hook can read the call.
This is the standard input that the command hook receives input from. The hook script reads the JSON here and makes a decision.
This is the number returned when the script ends. 0 means success, 2 means blocking, any other value is treated as a non-blocking error.

screens.outro: Now that we know the definition, let's check the timeline to see when the hook is executed.

screens.title: Hook types and execution time timeline
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to sequentially see when hooks occur from the beginning to the end of the session.

visual.alt: A horizontal timeline showing where hook events occur from the beginning to the end of a session.

steps.title: Session units: SessionStart, SessionEnd
steps.body: SessionStart occurs when the session starts and SessionEnd occurs when it ends. It is used to enter environmental information at the start of a session or to clean up at the end.

steps.title: By turn: UserPromptSubmit, Stop, StopFailure
steps.body: UserPromptSubmit fires before the user's prompt is processed, Stop fires when Claude finishes responding, and StopFailure fires when the turn ends with an API error. Used when checking a prompt or performing post-processing after responding.

steps.title: For each tool call: PreToolUse to PostToolUse
steps.body: Each tool call raises PreToolUse (before execution, can be prevented), PermissionRequest, PostToolUse (after success), and PostToolUseFailure (after failure). To prevent dangerous calls, use PreToolUse, which occurs before execution, and use PostToolUse for formatting and logging.

steps.title: any other point in time
steps.body: These include SubagentStart and SubagentStop, which indicate the start and end of subagents, PreCompact and PostCompact before and after context compression, ConfigChange when settings change, and FileChanged when files change.

steps.title: rules to remember
steps.body: PreToolUse and PostToolUse occur on each tool call, but the EndConversation call is skipped. If there are multiple hooks matching the same event, they will be executed in parallel.

screens.outro: Now that we've got the point, let's read the configuration structure and matcher.

screens.title: Hook configuration structure and matcher
screens.lead: Select a highlighted phrase in the settings below and the role each phrase plays in the hook action will be explained.

marks.note: Event name. Settings are nested under hooks in the following order: event name, matcher, and handler list. If the event name is incorrect, the hook will not run at all.

This is a condition that filters which target to react to. Tool events use the tool name. As long as it contains letters, numbers, underscores, hyphens, spaces, commas, and vertical lines, it will be interpreted as a list of exact names; any other characters will be interpreted as regular expressions. Forms such as Edit|Write or mcp__.* are possible.
This is the handler type. command executes a shell command or script and receives input through stdin.
Conditions that are further narrowed down to permission rule grammar. The script is only executed when both matcher and if match, reducing the cost of launching the script for every Bash call.

This is the script that actually runs. ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} points to the project base path. If you do not have execution permission, the hook will end with an error and the intended blocking will not occur.

screens.outro: Now that you've read the settings, let's see how the script returns results.

screens.title: Handling hook results: exit code and JSON
screens.lead: Read the script below to see how the hook returns a result. The explanation on the right also lists symptoms when results are handled incorrectly.

notes.note: Reads commands from tool input from JSON coming to stdin. This line works only if jq is installed. Without jq, the script will end with an error. Unless the exit code is 2, it is a non-blocking error and the dangerous command will be executed as is.

If rm -rf is present, it will output JSON, terminating with an exit code of 0. If permissionDecision is deny, the tool call is blocked, and permissionDecisionReason is passed to Claude to find another way. Prevent text other than JSON objects from being mixed in stdout.
Non-corresponding commands exit with exit code 0 and no output. This means there is no decision and it goes to the normal authority flow. Silence does not mean approval.

You can also use just the exit code. If it ends with 2, the call will be blocked in PreToolUse and stderr will be passed as the reason. Other exit codes are non-blocking errors. Choose only one exit code signal and one JSON method per hook. If shuffled, blocking with exit code 2 takes precedence.

screens.outro: Now that we know how to handle results, let's compare a table to see how hooks differ from other controls.

screens.title: Hooks and permission rules, ADK callbacks/plugins, inference hooks
screens.lead: Read the table and compare the roles that seemingly similar control measures are divided into.

data.caption: Control Measures Comparison
rows: permission rules
Declarative allow, confirm, deny
Look only for tool or command pattern matches.
If you simply deny or allow, for example Bash (aws *)
hook
Developer and project level automation
The code reads the input and makes decisions based on conditions.
Blocking according to command content, formatting and logging after execution
ADK callback/plugin
ADK intervention points
Validate arguments before and after model calls and tool calls.
Verification before and after invocation of agents created with ADK
Prompt/Agent Handler Hook
A handler that is evaluated once by the model or inspected by a subagent
Evaluate conditions that require judgment from a model instead of a script.
Semantic-based inspection that is difficult to write as a rule
Inference Hook (Enterprise)

All prompts and tool calls are sent to an organization-hosted server for allow or deny.

data.notes: Inference hooks run within the Claude infrastructure and do not depend on individual device settings, so they can be set up once across your entire organization. ADK callbacks and plugins have different names, but they are devices with the same purpose: intervening before and after model and tool calls. However, since the handler that leaves the decision to the model is not as definitive as the code, command hooks or deny rules are first considered for rules that must be blocked.

screens.outro: Now that we've compared the means, let's unravel step by step the flow that the hook blocks in the example.

screens.title: Explanatory example: Flow of blocking dangerous commands with a hook
screens.lead: The instructor explains the case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: Hook interpretation process: PreToolUse, matcher, if, script, decision flow.
labels: rm -rf with: deny, pass reason to Claude
Else: no decision, normal authority flow

steps.title: situation
steps.body: The agent tries to run the rm -rf /tmp/build command to clean up the build folder. The project has rules to prevent destructive delete commands. This call raises the PreToolUse event.

steps.title: Step 1: Narrow your target
steps.body: Add Bash as a matcher to PreToolUse, and Bash(rm *) as if. The script is executed only when both conditions match, so all other shell commands do not incur the cost of the hook.

steps.title: Step 2: Script reads commands
steps.body: The script reads tool_input.command from stdin. If rm -rf is present here, it will output JSON with permissionDecision set to deny. This decision is made by the code, not the model, so the result is always the same.

steps.title: Step 3: Reason is sent to Claude
steps.body: The reason written in permissionDecisionReason is sent to Claude. Claude realizes that the call is blocked and why, and finds a safer way. The more specific your reason, the better your next action will be.

steps.title: Step 4: Pass non-applicable commands
steps.body: Safe variants, such as rm file.txt, do not have rm -rf, so the script makes no decision and ends with exit code 0. In this case, it falls into the normal permission flow and is processed as usual.

steps.title: Step 5: Check the environmental assumptions first
steps.body: This script uses jq. If jq is not installed, the script will end with an error, and since it is not an exit code of 2, it will be a non-blocking error and the command will be executed as is. First check whether the hook works as intended and environmental conditions such as jq installation.

steps.title: organizing
steps.body: A hook is a device in which code intervenes immediately before tool execution, independent of the model's judgment. The target must be narrowed down to matcher and if, the result returned as JSON, and the environment premise must be checked for it to operate definitively.

screens.outro: Hooks aren't always the answer. Let's analyze which ones to block with hooks and which ones with rules.

screens.title: Analysis: What to block with hooks and what to block with permission rules
screens.lead: As you select each question, your judgment and reasons unfold. Decide for yourself first and then unfold it. There is nothing to enter or submit.

items.prompt: I want to block all aws commands. Do I need a hook?
items.answer: You don't need it. A deny rule is sufficient to simply deny a tool or command pattern. For example, in Bash (aws *) one line is all you need: The rules are declarative, making them easier to read and less prone to mistakes.

items.prompt: Among the rm commands, I want to block only rm -rf. What should I do?
items.answer: The hook is correct because you have to read the command and make a decision based on the conditions. If you block the entire rm with a deny rule, even safe rms will be denied. If you have the hook read commands from stdin and output deny only when rm -rf, you'll only block as much as you need.

items.prompt: What should I use to automatically run the formatter after editing a file?
items.answer: Post-execution post-processing is up to the PostToolUse hook. It runs immediately after a successful edit, so you don't have to ask the model to run the formatter and you don't miss anything.

items.prompt: How do you enforce a policy for all employees, regardless of device?
items.answer: Consider inference hooks. It is applied once to the entire organization rather than relying on personal device settings, and is used to prevent data leaks and enforce policies. Organizational level control assumed by the compliance team. It may be excessive for the needs of individual developers or project units, so choose a method that fits the scope.

Hooks run outside the sandbox as a local process. If a hook script handles external input, the script itself is also subject to safety checks. If you pass the input as is to the shell without verifying it, the hook becomes a path to danger. It's a good idea to keep hook scripts simple and short, and review them when changes are made.

screens.outro: Now that we have summarized the criteria for judgment, let’s gather the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Select a sentence and check the evidence
screens.lead: If you select each summary sentence, the evidence will unfold. There is nothing to enter or submit. It's a good idea to first say the meaning of the sentence yourself and then unfold it.

items.prompt: A hook is a handler that runs at a set point in time and can prevent tool calls from PreToolUse.
items.answer: There are multiple points per session, turn, and tool call, and the event that can be blocked before executing the tool is PreToolUse. PostToolUse occurs after success, so it fits post-processing.

items.prompt: Narrow the target using matcher and if, and return results as exit code or JSON output.
items.answer: matcher is the tool name, and if is the condition of the permission rule grammar. The result is returned as exit code 0, 2, or permissionDecision in JSON. This is an error in that a hook only selects one method and does not block abnormal terminations other than exit code 2. So, if blocking is absolutely necessary, you must end it with 2 or print deny JSON correctly.

items.prompt: A simple denial is a permission rule, a content-based judgment is a hook, and organization-wide enforcement is a reasoning hook.
items.answer: Rules are declarative, making them suitable for simple allow and deny, while hooks are code that reads input and makes conditional decisions. An inference hook is how the organization server returns allow or deny to all prompts and tool calls.

items.prompt: ADK callbacks and plugins are also devices for the same purpose, intervening before and after model and tool calls.
items.answer: ADK allows callbacks and plugins to validate arguments before and after model and tool calls. The name and setting method are different, but the same thing is that code intervenes independently of the model's judgment. No matter what product you use, it is helpful to first check where the intervention points are.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's think about it in relation to our own work.

screens.title: Connect to my work
screens.lead: This screen is for reading only. Read the questions and think for yourself. You will not enter or submit an answer.

paragraphs: Key terms in this lesson are Hooks, PreToolUse and PostToolUse, hook result processing, and inference hooks. Let's go back to the original question. At what point, what information do you receive, and how can you prevent it?

The starting point is PreToolUse just before tool execution, the information is a JSON context passed to stdin, and the blocking method is JSON output with permissionDecision set to deny or exit code 2. You need to know all three for the hook to work as intended. If even one thing is off, the hook quietly does nothing. So, whenever you change the settings, check it with a check call.

Thinking about the agent you are using, write down a list of calls that must be blocked and post-processing that must be performed. For each item on that list, you can consider whether rules are sufficient, whether hooks are needed, or whether organizational level controls are needed. In most cases, rules are sufficient, and hooks are simple to use only in cases that cannot be expressed in rules.

Lastly, once you've created a hook, get into the habit of checking to see if it's really stuck. Hooks are prone to silent failure. This is because if jq is missing or execution permission is missing, there may be no warning even though blocking does not occur. Hook's rationale is also subject to design. Rather than simply writing a ban, you can tell an alternative to use and the agent will quickly choose the correct method.

callout.label: Questions to Think About
callout.text: Where does my work get stuck with Hooks? If there is a rule you want to enforce in code rather than leaving it to the model's judgment, think of one.

checks.q: Match the next hook event with execution time
right: After the tool call is successful
Immediately before executing the tool, the call can be prevented
checks.explain: Hooks are executed at specified points in the life cycle. To prevent tool calls, you must use PreToolUse, which occurs before execution, and PostToolUse is suitable for post-processing such as formatting or logging.
checks.intro: Hook events are executed at specified points in the life cycle. Match events with points in time.
checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. You correctly connected the following points: before processing the prompt, immediately before and after executing the tool, and just before compression.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a pair whose viewpoints are misaligned. Note that the only thing that can block the call is PreToolUse before execution, and PostToolUse is for post-processing after success.

checks.q: The command script in the PreToolUse hook ended with exit code 1. What happens to tool calls?
options: The call is blocked, as with exit code 2
It is treated as a non-blocking error and the tool call proceeds as is.
Claude runs the same hook again until he succeeds.
The tool call is canceled and the session is terminated.
checks.explain: It is exit code 2 that causes blocking; other exit codes are non-blocking errors and the operation proceeds as is. To make sure you block it, end it with a 2 or end it with a 0 and output the deny decision as JSON.

wrong.0: Blocking is the action with exit code 2.
wrong.2: The hook will not be re-executed if it fails.
wrong.3: Non-blocking errors do not end the session.

checks.intro: See how the hook script's exit code affects tool calls.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Blocking the call is exit code 2, and 1 is a non-blocking error, so the tool call proceeds as is.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It's easy to think that exit code 1 is a failure and therefore blocked. Blocking only occurs when it is 2, and to make sure you block it, you must end it with 2 or end it with 0 and output deny as JSON.

checks.q: We want to block only shell commands executed by the agent that contain rm -rf, and allow other rm commands. What is the most appropriate means?
options: Write ‘Do not use dangerous commands’ in the prompt.
The PreToolUse hook reads the command contents from stdin and outputs deny only when rm -rf.
Turn on inference hooks to send all commands to the organization server
checks.explain: If you have to read the command and make a decision based on the conditions, the hook is correct. A deny rule is sufficient to simply deny a pattern, but it blocks the entire rm.

wrong.0: The entire rm command is blocked and other rm commands are also rejected.
wrong.1: There is no guarantee that the model will always follow the prompt instructions.
wrong.3: Inference hooks are organizational-level policy enforcement devices and are overkill for this requirement.

checks.intro: This is a request that should only be blocked by rm -rf. Choose a means to read and judge the content.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Since the command content must be read and judged based on conditions, a PreToolUse hook that reads stdin is appropriate.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The deny rule denies the entire pattern, thus blocking other rms, and the prompt instruction has no force. If you have to make a decision based on conditions, think of it as a hook.

glossary.def: A custom handler that runs automatically at certain points in the Claude Code life cycle. There are five types: command, http, mcp_tool, prompt, and agent.
An event that occurs before executing a tool call (blockable) and after success.
Exit code 0 is success, 2 is blocking, and anything else is a non-blocking error. Sophisticated control is achieved through JSON output.
A field that filters what the hook will respond to, for example the tool name. You can narrow it down further by if.
Organization-level control in the Enterprise plan that directs all prompts and tool calls to the organization server for allow or deny.

misconceptions.myth: Hooks ensure that the model always follows the rules.
misconceptions.fact: A hook is not a model, but a device through which code intervenes at the time of tool execution. The model still tries to make the call, and the hook prevents the call.

misconceptions.myth: The hook blocks the tool in case of any abnormal termination.
misconceptions.fact: Only exit code 2 is blocked. Any other exit code is a non-blocking error and the tool call proceeds as is.

misconceptions.myth: Hooks and permission rules serve the same purpose, so you only need one.
misconceptions.fact: Simple rejection is a rule, and conditional judgment based on content is a hook. The two have different roles and are often used together.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: A hook is a handler that runs at a set point in time and can prevent tool calls from PreToolUse.
Narrow the target with matchers and ifs, and return results as exit codes or JSON output.
Simple denial is handled by permission rules, content-based judgment is handled by hooks, and organization-wide enforcement is handled by inference hooks.
ADK's callbacks and plugins are also devices for the same purpose, intervening before and after model and tool calls.
